extracted.intended_audience: aspiring sketch comedy writers, SNL fans, and readers curious about television writing/production
extracted.subtask_description: A week-by-week description of how Saturday Night Live develops, selects, rewrites, and produces sketches for the live show — covering meetings, writing nights, read-throughs, rehearsals, and production constraints. Useful for people trying to understand or emulate SNL's sketch-writing and production cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monday pitch meeting (cast, writers, producers, host)
rubrics_metrics.description: Production normally starts on Monday with a free-form pitch meeting between the cast, writers, producers including Lorne Michaels, and the guest host, in Michael’s office, over two hours. The host is invited to pitch ideas during this meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This meeting is primarily for pitching ideas rather than heavy sketch writing. Host participation matters — they can influence which sketches move forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host input / host has the most say
rubrics_metrics.description: The host generally has the most say and input in what sketches they want to be in; the host is invited to pitch and their preferences influence selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Host buy-in can make or break a sketch's chances; writers should tailor pitches to host strengths and likely participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tuesday — dedicated writing day and late-night tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Tuesday is the only day dedicated purely to writing the scripts, a process which can extend through the night into Wednesday. Writing may not begin until late afternoon/evening and can continue into the early morning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SNL operates with a tradition of late-night, high-intensity writing sessions (examples: people staying until 4 a.m., sleeping on couches). Productivity is judged by output (strong pieces) rather than hours alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script formatting and submission deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Pieces just have to be in and formatted by the script department by the read-through (the read-through is usually around 2:30 p.m. on Wednesday).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meeting formatting and submission deadlines is mandatory — late or unformatted pieces risk not being considered. The script department enforces the entry standard for read-through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wednesday read-through evaluation (separate weak from strong)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the Wednesday read-through sketches are read in turn (~40 ideas), attended by writers, producers, cast, and technical experts; the read-through separates the weak from the strong. Strong pieces are fast-tracked while weak ones are killed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read-throughs are lengthy and public; performance of the piece at read-through and immediate reception determine advancement. Expect a large, multi-hour evaluation with many stakeholders present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/feasibility input during read-through
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical experts such as make-up artists, who may be required to realize certain sketch ideas (e.g., those using prosthetics), attend the read-through to advise on feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches requiring complex props, prosthetics, or special effects are vetted early for practicality; logistical concerns can limit a sketch's viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and show layout decided by Michaels and producers
rubrics_metrics.description: After the read-through, Michaels, the head writer, the guest host, and some producers decide the layout of the show and which sketches will be developed for air. Writers and cast are then informed whether their sketch survived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers convene separately to build the show; being selected to be developed depends on these producers' judgment of quality, fit, and feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thursday — rehearsals and rewrites
rubrics_metrics.description: Thursday is rehearsal and a bunch of rewrites; sketches may be rewritten starting the same day and work focuses on developing and rewriting the remaining sketches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect iterative changes as sketches are refined; initial drafts can be substantially altered between read-through and rehearsal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friday — collaboration with production departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Friday sketch writers work with set builders, costume designers and musicians trying to make their ideas come to life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close collaboration with technical departments is required; writers must adapt ideas to production realities (sets, costumes, music).

rubrics_metrics.name: Saturday — dress rehearsals and last-minute decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Saturday involves lots of dress rehearsals where last minute decisions get made; the opening monologue can be written as late as Saturday afternoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final lineup and material can still change at dress rehearsals; time-sensitive or late-arriving material may be accepted if it proves strong in rehearsal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show length constraint (90-minute runtime)
rubrics_metrics.description: Michaels reviews the show lineup to ensure it meets a 90-minute length, and sketches that have made it as far as the live rehearsal may be removed to meet this limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Runtime constraints are a hard production limit — even rehearsed sketches can be cut for time. Writers should account for pacing and length when crafting pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekend Update team workflow and host coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: The three- to four-member dedicated 'Weekend Update' writing team writes jokes throughout the week. Hosts normally do not work with or read the team's scripts until Thursday evening, after main show sketches are finalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weekend Update operates on a parallel but slightly separate schedule; hosts provide input late in the week and may contribute to the script then.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea quality over personality
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea and the piece is what dominates more than the personality in a lot of cases — great pieces will be accepted regardless of when or how they were written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing a strong, funny idea is the primary currency; unconventional hours or personal style matter less than the strength of the sketch itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiring and cultural expectation (first-TV-job ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lorne Michaels has a strong belief in hiring people for their first television job at SNL; many practices are counterintuitive to people who worked elsewhere, and the show values tradition and adaptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New hires should expect to adapt to SNL's idiosyncratic workflows and traditions; being open to the show's established pace and methods is part of succeeding there.
